It depends on the state, but in Arizona you just tell the state your party affiliation to vote in either the Republican or Democrat Primary. Your voter card shows party affiliation (which can even be independent). And then in some states, an Independent party affiliation means you can still just choose one Primary to vote in, but it's generally safer to just change your voter card. When the actual election comes, you can still vote the Republican candidate even if you're a Democrat, or vice-versa.

Each party has a primary election to select the candidate they want to run in the general election. Only party members can vote in their own party's primary but everyone can vote in the general election. So the democrats will have a primary where they choose between Hillary, Bernie, and whoever else and the republicans will have a primary to choose between Jeb, Trump, and whoever else decides to run. The winners of the primaries will then run against each other in the general election. (Third parties like the green party and libertarians will run people too but they generally don't get many votes)

People identify as either republican or democrat because they view the system as only giving one of those two a chance. A lot of people will say something like "I would vote libertarian but that would just mean I'm tossing my vote away on a lost cause and republicans get one less vote, meaning the democrat I like less than the republicans has a better chance of getting elected"

I'm not sure I agree with these things being called holograms. It's not truly making a 3D image. It is making the illusion of one, because you can move around the "image" and see the different sides. But you cannot move your POV above the image. As soon as you go top-down on your phone, you just see 4 images on your phone, and the plastic device. It doesn't merge them together and allow for full movement around the image, like this or (less impressive) this. You're simply putting 4 stationary POVs on 4 different planes that the end user can circle around. Neat trick, but not a Hologram, IMHO.

Yeah, not a hologram at all. It's an old stage trick that's been used in theater since the 19th century but that won't stop people from calling it a hologram.

As an aside for those who are interested, you don't need a 3D printer to make one. A few nights ago I made one with scissors, scotch tape, and some clear plastic like the kind those un-openable clamshell electronics packages are made from.

Cut out four equilateral triangles, cut one corner off of each triangle, and tape them together! Good way to kill a few minutes with the kids.

The pepper ghost effect is really 3D, as it's the reflection of a 3D object therefore has parallax, and each eye sees different angle, has depth, and so on.

This one is just the reflection of a 2D image. Although being a reflection does trick your brain a bit (I guess because it seems to be floating mid-air), it lacks all other characteristics of the pepper ghost effect.
